A region in the $x$-$y$ plane is bounded by the curve $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{x}$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=1$ and $x=\pi $, as shown above. The area of the region is
questions.worked_solution:
To find the area, we just need to compute the corresponding definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{ln}⁡x){|}_{1}^{\pi } \\  & =(-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi )-(-\operatorname{cos}⁡1+\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =1+\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡1.\end{aligned}
$$

A region in the $x$-$y$ plane is bounded by the curve $y={sec}^{2}⁡x+\frac{1}{x}$, and the $x$-axis between $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$ and $x=\frac{\pi }{3}$, as shown above. 
Find the area $A$ of the region. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the area, we just need to compute the corresponding definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}({sec}^{2}⁡(x)+\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{sec}^{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x\,+\,{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)){|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3} \\  & =(\operatorname{tan}⁡\frac{\pi }{3}+\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{\pi }{3})-(\operatorname{tan}⁡\frac{\pi }{6}+\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\sqrt{3}+\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}-\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}+\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{\pi /3}{\pi /6} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area between the curve $y=-3{x}^{2}+5x$, the $x$-axis and the line $x=1$, shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the area, we just need to compute the corresponding definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-3{x}^{2}+5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+5\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3\cdot {\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1}+5\cdot {\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-3(\frac{1}{3}-0)+5(\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area of the closed region between the curve $y=4-{x}^{2}$ and the $x$-axis, shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the area, we just need to compute the corresponding definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}(4-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{-2}^{2}\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4x{|}_{-2}^{2}-{\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}|}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =4(2-(-2))-(\frac{8}{3}-(-\frac{8}{3})) \\  & =16-\frac{16}{3} \\  & =\frac{32}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
To find the area, we just need to compute the corresponding definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{1}{8}{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot {\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(\frac{(2)^{4}}{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(4) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area $A$ between the curve $y=-{x}^{2}-8$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=0$ and $x=2$ (shown above). Do not round the answer.

$A=$ 
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the area, we just need to compute the corresponding definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-{x}^{2}-8)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-8{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{2}-8\cdot x{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =-(\frac{(2)^{3}}{3}-0)-8(2-0) \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}-16 \\  & =-\frac{56}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we obtained a negative number. So the area that we want is 

$$
A=-{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{56}{3}.
$$

A region is bounded by the curve $y=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}$, the $x$-axis, and the lines $x=0$ and $x=\frac{3}{2}$, as shown above. Find the area $A$ of the region. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the area, we just need to compute the corresponding definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3/2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =arccos\,(\frac{x}{3}){|}_{0}^{3/2} \\  & =arccos\,(\frac{1}{2})-arccos\,(0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we obtained a negative number. So the area that we want is 

$$
A=-{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\pi }{6}.
$$

A region is bounded by the curve $y=-\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x=0$ and $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$, as shown above. Find the area of the region.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the area, we just need to compute the corresponding definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(-\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{sec}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =-(\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sec}⁡0) \\  & =-(\sqrt{2}-1) \\  & =1-\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we obtained a negative number. So the area that we want is $\sqrt{2}-1.$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the area between the curve $y=x^2-2x+2,$ the $x$-axis, and the lines $x=0$ and $x=2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040771/assets/6b85f10cde49017eac1c56ad1b8abbcdf3033a367d5e1eb162dd89fbb6141461.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the area, we just need to compute the corresponding definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{2}-2x+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-2{\int }_{0}^{2}x\,\text{d}x+2{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{2}-2\cdot {\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{2}+2x{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{8}{3}-0)-2(2-0)+2(2-0) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}-4+4 \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the area of the closed region between the curve $y=x^2-1$ and the $x$-axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-1 & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

We draw a sketch of the region, as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040771/assets/9b78aad41f84f6a6997914bd8d4243f30cb0ebea4edb5305962dc11c7a46a807.png)

We want the area between the curve $y=x^2-1$ and the $x$-axis, from $x=-1$ to $x=1.$ To find the area, we just need to compute the corresponding definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{-1}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}|}_{-1}^{1}-x{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-(-\frac{1}{3}))-(1-(-1)) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-2 \\  & =-\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we obtained a negative number. So the area that we want is $\dfrac{4}{3}.$
